consensus_summary: Egypt primarily and settledly symbolizes bondage/slavery to sin and the oppressive godless world-system, with the Exodus as the paradigm of deliverance; secondary strands include false security, refuge/preservation, imperial pride, and (via Rev 11:8) the hostile ‘world city’ that some apply to unfaithful Jerusalem.
book_summary: Spiritually Egypt is the whore of Babylon that rides the beast—the city that kills the prophets, where also our Lord was crucified: Jerusalem.
consensus_core_identification: bondage to sin / the oppressive world-system (Exodus house of slavery)
book_core_identification: Jerusalem (whore of Babylon / city that kills the prophets)
boundary_disagreement: Consensus centers the symbol on the general condition of bondage and the world-system (Jerusalem appearing only as an occasional secondary application of the Rev 11:8 epithet); the book reassigns the spiritual meaning of Egypt wholly and exclusively to the concrete city of Jerusalem.
material_contradiction: The core symbolic referent cannot be both the abstract state/system of bondage-to-sin (consensus primary) and the historical city of Jerusalem (book); accepting the book’s identification replaces rather than qualifies the consensus core.
rationale: Minimum cores differ in kind: consensus (all three responses) locks the primary identification to the Exodus bondage typology applied to sin/world; the book instead equates spiritual Egypt with Jerusalem via Rev 11:8 and related texts. Although Response A notes that some interpreters apply the Rev 11:8 ‘world city’ epithet to unfaithful Jerusalem, that remains a listed alternative of secondary prominence, not the settled core. The book therefore replaces the consensus referent rather than narrowing, broadening, or overlapping within the same category.
strongest_objection: The dominant biblical usage and the entire Christian interpretive tradition (patristic through modern) treat Egypt as the paradigmatic house of bondage; Rev 11:8 is a single metaphorical transfer of the name, not a redefinition of the symbol’s core meaning as Jerusalem.
